docs.b: Our Story Started with a die. Still extruding every profile. American Pro is the building products line of Patwin Plastics, a family-run American PVC extruder founded in 1971 by tool and die maker Thomas Hannen. Five decades on, the same family still runs the plant and makes every American Pro product in-house. How we got here A toolmaker, a die, and the rest is extrusion. In 1971, Thomas Hannen , a tool and die maker by trade, founded Patwin Plastics . Thomas understood something most people didn't: the die is the heart of any extrusion. Get the die right and the profile takes care of itself. He started by running OEM profiles like T-molding, U-channels, and bumper molding for customers who needed precise, repeatable parts. Outwater Plastics became one of the earliest distribution partners and still moves Patwin product today. Most of what we extruded in those early decades shipped under someone else's name, into the furniture industry, into point-of-purchase displays, into the back of products you'd recognize without ever knowing we made the part. In the late 1990s we asked a different question: what else can we make? The answer turned out to be fencing, then decking, then mouldings, railings, siding, and porch flooring. American Pro Building Products launched in 2001 as the brand for the building products line, the first time finished product ever shipped under our own name. Still in the family Patwin is run today by Thomas's sons, Timothy Hannen and Thomas Hannen Jr. , with the next generation of the family already coming up through the business. The plant has changed. The ownership structure hasn't. What we believe Most of what we make still doesn't carry our name. American Pro is what we ship under our own banner: the cellular PVC products we'd install on our own homes. We don't chase trends. We cut dies, run extrusions, ship on time, and stand behind every linear foot. Fifty-plus years in, the same family is still running the plant. docs.t: Choosing Crown Moulding Size and Profile. A Homeowner's Guide.
docs.d: American Pro cuts PVC crown moulding in five standard sizes, from 2 3/4 inch to 8 inch, plus Solid Crown, Rams Crown, and Rake Mold. How to match crown size to eave depth and roofline, when to step up to a two-piece build-up, and how casing, brick mould, and sill profiles complete the look.

docs.b: The crown does more work than any other piece of trim on the house. Get the size wrong and everything under it looks off. Crown moulding is the trim that sets the scale of a house before anyone consciously notices it. Too small under a deep overhang and the roofline looks unfinished. Too large on a modest single story and the house looks like it is wearing someone else's coat. Getting it right is not about picking a favorite profile from a catalog page. It is arithmetic: eave depth, wall height, and how far back you stand to look at it. American Pro cuts PVC crown in five standard sizes plus three specialty crown profiles, all extruded in-house at Patwin Plastics in Linden, New Jersey. Here is how to read your own roofline and land on the right one, plus how casing, brick mould, and sill tie into the same decision. Start with the overhang, not the room Interior crown gets sized to ceiling height. Exterior crown gets sized to the depth of the eave and fascia it sits under, and to how far the wall it wraps sits from the street or the walkway. A crown that looks correct tucked under a 6 inch fascia on a one-story cottage will look thin and lost under a 10 inch overhang on a two-story colonial with tall first-floor windows. The house tells you the size before the spec sheet does. 2 3/4" Cottages, single story, shallow eaves 3 5/8" Ranch and modest two-story homes 4 5/8" Most colonial and craftsman homes 5 1/4" Deep eaves, tall pilasters 8" Porticos, entries meant to be seen from the street Those are starting points, not rules. A 4 5/8 inch crown on a small farmhouse porch can look correct if the porch has tall square columns and a deep frieze board above them. The same crown on a low ranch with a narrow fascia will look oversized. Stand where a visitor stands, at the front walk or the curb, and judge scale from there rather than up close on a ladder. The full standard catalog, not just crown Crown gets the attention, but it rarely works alone. docs.d: Three ways to fasten a deck board compared: face screwed and left bare, face screwed with color-matched Starborn Pro Plug plugs, and hidden clips on InvisiClip. Appearance, water intrusion, board movement, install labor, repairs, and tested uplift on American Pro PVC decking.

docs.b: The decision gets made right here, board by board, and it is usually made in about ten seconds. Every deck gets fastened one of two ways. Either the screws go down through the face of the board, or the hardware goes underneath it in a groove. That is the whole decision, and it is usually made in about ten seconds on a job site. It deserves longer than that, because it is the one choice that touches how the deck looks, how it drains, how it moves, how long it takes to build, and how you fix it in year eight. Here is the honest comparison. Not a sales page, a spec discussion. Where face screwing wins, it wins, and we will say so. Start with the arithmetic Face screwing is not two screws. It is two screws per board, per joist, for every board on the deck. Run 5.5 inch boards over a frame at 16 inches on center and that works out to roughly three fasteners in every square foot of finished deck. A 400 square foot deck carries well over a thousand visible screw heads. Each one is a hole drilled through the wear surface of the board, and each one has to be driven to the right depth, in line with its neighbor, without mushrooming the material around it. ~3 Face screws per square foot 1,200+ Screw heads on a 400 sq ft deck 0 Visible fasteners with InvisiClip™ How that math works 5.5 in. board width by 16 in. joist spacing is 0.61 sq ft of deck per board, per joist bay. Two screws across that area is about 3.3 fasteners per square foot. Tighten the joist spacing or narrow the board and the count goes up, not down. Appearance is the obvious one, and it is not the important one A grid of screw heads is the first thing anyone notices, and on a premium wood-grain board it is the thing that gives away the price of the deck. Our boards are built to look like lumber, with a five-layer RENOLIT PMMA film over a proprietary ASA capstock, and a thousand stainless dots read straight through that work. If you want to see how much detail is in the surface, the board construction breakdown covers what is actually under your feet. But appearance is the argument everyone already knows. The reasons that matter show up later. A bare screw head is a hole in the wear surface A countersunk screw head sits in a shallow dish. docs.d: InvisiClip™ is American Pro's hidden fastener system for grooved PVC decking. POM clips snap onto aluminum rails, boards drop in from above, no screws on the deck surface. Powered by the GRAD® system.

docs.b: InvisiClip™ in detail. POM clip on aluminum rail, grooved board ready to drop. We are launching InvisiClip™, the hidden fastener system we have paired with our grooved PVC decking. It is the quietest piece of hardware on a deck, and the most consequential. The clip disappears under the board, the rail disappears on top of the joist, and the deck finally gets to look like the deck. InvisiClip™ is the GRAD® system, the European-engineered hidden clip platform that has been quietly setting decks for years. We chose it, we tested it on our boards, and we stand behind it. Here is what it is, why we picked it, and where to see it. What it is InvisiClip™ is a three-part system. POM polymer clips snap onto pre-fabricated aluminum rails. The rails sit on top of every joist, running parallel to the joists, at 16 inches on center maximum. Grooved for InvisiClip™ deck boards drop in from above. The two channels on the underside of each board catch the clips. Done. There are no screws on the finished deck surface. No plugs. No countersinks. No future stain rings. The board face leaves the mill the way you ordered it, and that is the way it stays. Because InvisiClip™ is the GRAD® system under our label, every install detail from the published GRAD method carries over. Installer training, install guides, and the Grad keys already on the truck all work the same way they always have. Why this system Top-fastened decks tell on themselves. Every screw head is a future stain ring, a UV halo, a place for water to pool. Hidden fasteners look better the day they go in, and they keep looking better through every season after. Patwin Plastics has been extruding precision PVC profiles in-house since 1971. We mix our own compound, cut our own dies, and run our own tooling for the boards. When it came to the hidden clip, we did not want to reinvent something that already worked. We evaluated the field, picked the GRAD® system, tested it on our decking, and brought it to market under the InvisiClip™ name. The clean deck doesn't show its work. Engineered for our decking InvisiClip™ is designed to fit the American Pro Grooved for InvisiClip™ deck board profile and any board manufactured to the GRAD® system profile. docs.d: American Pro grooved decking on InvisiClip™ was tested by Intertek under ICC-ES AC174 using ASTM E330. Three specimens averaged 306 psf ultimate uplift. Here is what that number means for a hidden-fastener deck in a high-wind or coastal setting.
docs.h: What the numbers say | Why we tested it at all | What it means on a real deck | The short version
docs.b: American Pro decking in Aged Oak on InvisiClip™. A hidden-fastener deck only looks effortless. Underneath, the clip and rail carry the load. A hidden-fastener deck raises a fair question. If there are no screws on the surface, what is holding the boards down when the wind gets under them? (For the wider comparison, see hidden fasteners vs face screwing .) On an exposed deck, a rooftop terrace, or anything near the water, that is not a small question. So we sent InvisiClip™ to an independent lab and had it pulled apart on purpose. American Pro grooved decking installed with InvisiClip™ was tested by Intertek Building & Construction under the ICC-ES AC174 acceptance criteria, using the ASTM E330 test method for structural performance under uniform static air-pressure difference. Here is what came back, and what the numbers actually mean for a deck you can stand on. 306 psf Average ultimate uplift 292 psf Average sustained uplift 3 Specimens tested What the numbers say Uplift is measured in pounds per square foot, or psf. It is the amount of upward pressure the assembly can take before the boards let go of the clips. Across three separate specimens, the InvisiClip™ assembly reached an average ultimate uplift of 306 psf. The sustained figure, 292 psf, is the load it held for a full ten-second hold before the clips released. For context, wind pressure on a low deck surface in most residential settings is a small fraction of that. These are large margins, and they were achieved with the same clips and the same aluminum rails you would order for any American Pro grooved deck. Nothing in the test assembly was special. That is the point of the test. The test specimen at Intertek. Rails on joists, boards clipped in, mounted over a sealed chamber that pulls the assembly upward until the clips release. Why we tested it at all InvisiClip™ is powered by the GRAD® system, a hidden-clip platform that has been setting decks in Europe for years. We could have pointed at that track record and left it there. We did not, because our boards are our boards. The groove geometry is extruded on our grooved TrueGrain Deck™ and grooved Legacy PVC decking, and the only honest way to know how our board and this clip behave together is to test the two of them as one assembly. docs.t: A Lakeside Deck in Aged Oak, with Nothing on the Surface but the View
docs.d: A tired wood deck on a New England lake gets rebuilt in TrueGrain Deck Aged Oak with InvisiClip hidden fasteners. No screws on the surface, no splinters underfoot, and a floor that stays cool at golden hour. The project, the choices, and the finished result.

docs.b: TrueGrain Deck in Aged Oak, hidden-fastened with InvisiClip. Golden hour on the lake. The old deck was doing what every wood deck does at year fifteen. Graying at the edges, cupping a little near the water, and giving up a splinter every time someone crossed it barefoot on the way to the lake. It had a good view and a bad floor. The goal for the rebuild was simple to say and harder to do. Keep the view. Fix the floor. And make it a surface nobody has to think about again. The homeowners picked TrueGrain Deck in Aged Oak , fastened with InvisiClip , so the finished floor shows the wood grain and the water, and nothing else. Why Aged Oak Color on a lake is a lighting decision as much as a taste one. The site faces west, so the deck gets full afternoon sun and then a long golden hour off the water. Very dark boards would have looked heavy in that light, and they run hotter underfoot in July. Aged Oak lands in the middle. A warm, weathered brown with real grain movement, so it reads natural against pine and stone without going orange. TrueGrain Deck earns that look honestly. It is a five-layer RENOLIT PMMA film over a proprietary ASA capstock over a cellular PVC core, which is why the grain has depth instead of a printed-on repeat. If you want the full construction story, we wrote it up in Inside TrueGrain Deck . The best compliment a new deck can get is that it looks like it was always there. The part you do not see The detail that makes this deck feel calm is the one you cannot point to. There are no screws on the surface. The boards were set with InvisiClip , our hidden fastener system built on the proven GRAD® platform. POM clips ride on aluminum rails, the grooved boards drop in from above, and the fasteners disappear under the deck line. No proud screws, no counterbored plugs working loose over the seasons. Consistent gaps. The rail system sets spacing for you, so the reveal between boards stays even the length of the deck. docs.b: Legacy PVC in Khaki. Solid color runs all the way through the board, so the tone you pick is the tone that lasts. Legacy PVC Decking is the original American Pro deck board. Solid-color, UV-stabilized cellular PVC with a subtle wood-grain texture, extruded on the same line as our flagship TrueGrain Deck at Patwin Plastics in Linden, New Jersey. The chemistry is identical. The difference is the finish: TrueGrain wears a laminated hardwood-grain surface, and Legacy wears a clean, classic color that goes straight through the board. That last part matters more than any single color name. Because Legacy is solid color all the way through, a saw cut, a stair nose, or a Pro Plug screw hole exposes the same tone as the surface. There is no printed film to wear off and no core color to surprise you at the end of a board. The color you choose is the color the deck stays. There are six of them. Here is what each one actually reads like once it is down and in daylight, and how to think about the choice for your home. Driftwood Light grey wood-grain Khaki Warm tan Hazelnut Medium warm brown Beachwood Cool grey grain Chestnut Rich red-brown Redwood Warm reddish-brown The two greys Driftwood Driftwood is the lighter of the two greys, a soft, sun-bleached tone with a light wood-grain figure running through it. It reads coastal without being cold. On a white or light-siding home it disappears into the architecture in the best way, letting the railing, the water, or the landscaping carry the eye. It is the color that photographs like weathered cedar that never actually weathered. Beachwood Beachwood is the cooler, deeper grey. Where Driftwood leans pale and sandy, Beachwood carries more depth and a truer grey cast with a defined grain. It is the right call when you want the modern grey deck look but do not want the surface to feel washed out, and it pairs cleanly with black railing, dark siding, and stone. If you are choosing between the two greys, think of Driftwood as beach house and Beachwood as contemporary. It is a warm tan, light enough to stay cool underfoot and neutral enough to sit under almost any siding color. docs.b: A walnut grooved board on the cooling line, fresh out of the die. Linden, NJ. Most decking sites tell you what their product looks like. Fewer tell you where it comes from. American Pro PVC decking, porch flooring, and architectural mouldings are extruded by Patwin Plastics on a Linden, New Jersey production floor. The compound is mixed in-house. The dies are cut in-house. The tooling that runs the boards is ours. That sentence is short, and it costs us money to be able to write it. What "made in Linden" actually means Patwin Plastics has been extruding precision PVC profiles since 1971. The decking and porch lines we run for American Pro use the same discipline that runs our other industrial profiles, just dressed for a backyard. The practical version, in plain English: Compound mixed on site. We blend our own PVC formulation rather than buying pre-pelletized resin from a third party. That means we control the additive package, the impact modifier, the UV stabilizer, and the color. Dies cut on site. When a profile needs to change for a new groove geometry, a thicker wall, or a tighter tolerance, we cut the die in-house. Faster turnaround. Tighter control on the part that actually shapes the board. Tooling and runs are ours. The lines that make American Pro decking are not rented runs on someone else's schedule. They are our extrusion lines, scheduled by our team, tied to our QC. Inspection happens on the line. Boards are checked for groove geometry, board straightness, color match, and surface finish before they leave Linden. We do not just badge a board. We extrude it. The brick mould around a front door. The sill under a kitchen window. On a lot of houses, those pieces are quietly rotting from the inside, and the homeowner has no idea until a finger goes through the paint. PVC mouldings don't do that. They don't drink water, so they can't rot. That single sentence is the entire reason architectural PVC moulding exists, and it changes how a house ages. Water gets in. The paint film slows it down, but it doesn't stop it. Once moisture is behind the film, three things start happening at once: Fungi feed on the cellulose. Wood rot is a biological process. Spores are everywhere. They just need food and moisture. Freeze-thaw cracks the wood. Water expands when it freezes. Every winter widens the gap between the paint and the wood. Insects find the soft spot. Carpenter ants and termites don't make rot, they exploit it. Wet wood is easy wood. The worst offenders are the parts of the house that get wet on purpose: brick mould around exterior doors, sills under windows that catch every storm, frieze and crown that sit just below a problem gutter, and water table that lives where siding meets foundation. docs.d: A porch floor sits under a roofline that funnels rainwater and snowmelt straight at it. Why water resistant materials like wood and composite eventually fail there, and how tongue-and-groove cellular PVC porch flooring is built to be fully waterproof.

Most homeowners assume a porch floor is a drier job than a deck. It has a roof over it. It is not standing wide open to every storm the way a deck is. That assumption is backward. A covered porch floor sits directly under a roofline that catches rainwater and snowmelt and funnels it, at volume, onto the same few boards, over and over, for the life of the house. That is a harder water problem than an open deck ever sees, and it is why the material underfoot needs to be waterproof, not just water resistant. Water resistant and waterproof are not the same claim Water resistant means a material slows down moisture absorption for a while. Waterproof means the material has nothing in it for water to absorb in the first place. That difference sounds academic until you look at what is actually happening underneath a painted or sealed porch floor. Sealed wood and capped wood plastic composite are both water resistant. A topical sealant, paint film, or polymer cap sits on the surface and pushes water off as long as that layer stays intact. Foot traffic, furniture legs, seasonal moisture cycling, and UV exposure all wear at that layer over years. Once it cracks, thins, or gets scratched through, the wood fiber underneath, whether it is solid lumber or the fiber blended into a composite core, starts absorbing water directly. From there it is only a matter of time before that moisture shows up as cupping, swelling, staining, or rot, usually starting exactly where you would expect: at the seams. The tongue-and-groove seam is where it starts Porch flooring is almost always installed tongue-and-groove, both for the tight, finished look and because it is how porch floors have been built for a century. That interlocking profile is also the part of the floor most exposed to trapped moisture. Water that lands on the surface works into the seam between boards and sits there, against two edges at once, far longer than it would sit on an open, gapped deck board that dries from both sides. On a water resistant material, that is a slow-motion failure point. What actually heats a deck A deck board sitting in direct sun is doing three things with solar energy at the same time. A cap engineered to reflect more of that invisible portion runs cooler than a color swatch alone would predict. How fast heat moves through the board. docs.b: Decking 101 What is cellular PVC decking? New to the term? Cellular PVC decking is a deck board made from foamed PVC with no wood fiber, which is why it won't rot, swell, or splinter. Here's a plain-English guide to how it's made, how it compares to composite, and whether it's worth the premium. Order Free Samples Try the 3D Deck Builder Cellular PVC decking is a deck board made from polyvinyl chloride with a closed-cell foamed structure and no wood fiber. The foamed core keeps it lighter and easier to work than solid PVC while staying stiff and strong, and because there is no wood content, water has no path into the board. That is why it won't rot, swell, or splinter. docs.t: What is cellular PVC decking?
docs.p: What Is Cellular PVC Decking? A Plain-English Guide
docs.d: Cellular PVC decking is a deck board made from polyvinyl chloride with a closed-cell foamed structure, which makes it lighter and easier to work than solid PVC while staying stiff and strong. Because it contains no wood fiber, water has no path into the board, so cellular PVC won't rot, swell, or splinter. Premium versions add a weatherable cap and a wood-grain surface.

docs.t: What is the difference between cellular PVC and composite decking?
docs.p: What Is Cellular PVC Decking? A Plain-English Guide
docs.d: Composite decking blends wood flour or fiber with plastic, so it still contains wood content that can absorb moisture, swell, stain, and fade. Cellular PVC has no wood fiber at all, so there is no moisture path anywhere in the board, including at cut ends and fastener holes. Cellular PVC also tends to run cooler underfoot than dark composite when it uses a reflective cap.

docs.t: How is cellular PVC decking made?
docs.p: What Is Cellular PVC Decking? A Plain-English Guide
docs.d: Cellular PVC decking is extruded: PVC compound is foamed to a controlled closed-cell density and pushed through a die that forms the board profile. Premium boards are capped, meaning a weatherable ASA layer is co-extruded over the core, and some, like TrueGrain, add a laminated wood-grain surface. American Pro's boards are extruded by Patwin Plastics in Linden, NJ.

docs.t: Does cellular PVC decking get hot?
docs.p: What Is Cellular PVC Decking? A Plain-English Guide
docs.d: Any decking warms in direct sun, and darker colors always run warmer than lighter ones. Cellular PVC with a reflective cap generally stays cooler than dark composite. TrueGrain Deck uses a cool-deck formulation that reflects more solar energy than dark composite, so lighter colorways stay more comfortable through the hottest part of the afternoon.

docs.t: Is cellular PVC decking worth it?
docs.p: What Is Cellular PVC Decking? A Plain-English Guide
docs.d: For homeowners who want the lowest long-term maintenance, cellular PVC is worth the premium. It never needs sanding, staining, or sealing, won't rot or splinter, and resists the moisture damage that shortens a wood or composite deck's life. American Pro cellular PVC carries a 25-year limited residential warranty and cleans with just soap and water.

docs.b: Installation Guide How to install PVC porch flooring. American Pro tongue-and-groove cellular PVC porch flooring installs the same way wood porch flooring has for a century, with the tools your installer already owns. Here is the step-by-step, from framing and slope through fastening and the final board. To install PVC porch flooring, joist spacing depends on board thickness: 3/4 inch porch flooring is rated for joists spaced up to 12 inches on center, and 1 inch nominal (7/8 inch actual) porch flooring is rated for joists spaced up to 16 inches on center. Slope the joists 1/4 inch per foot away from the structure. Start with the groove side against the structure, face-fasten the first board near the structure, then drive a fastener through the tongue at each joist at a 30 to 45 degree angle. Slide each following board's groove over the previous tongue, keep the top gap consistent, and rip the final board to width. Install boards as soon as possible after cutting to avoid temperature changes. If you must install below 32 degrees F, which is not recommended, leave a 1/16 inch gap, and avoid installing at high temperatures.

docs.t: What is InvisiClip™?
docs.p: InvisiClip™ Hidden Fastener System (Grad System)
docs.d: InvisiClip™ is American Pro's hidden fastener system for grooved PVC decking, powered by the Grad System. Engineered POM polymer clips snap onto aluminum rails. The rails sit on top of each joist running parallel to the joists at 16 inches on center maximum. Boards drop in from above so no screws or fasteners show on the finished deck.

docs.t: What spec does InvisiClip™ follow?
docs.p: InvisiClip™ Hidden Fastener System (Grad System)
docs.d: InvisiClip™ follows the Grad System component spec. The clips, rails, and accessories are dimensionally compatible with the published Grad install method. On American Pro decking, joists must be 16 inches on center maximum and a rail sits on top of every joist, so rails are also 16 inches on center maximum. Start Rail and Mini Rail fastener layouts and removability with Grad keys are unchanged.

docs.t: Are the deck boards removable after install?
docs.p: InvisiClip™ Hidden Fastener System (Grad System)
docs.d: Yes. Boards installed on InvisiClip™ Start Rails can be lifted out individually using Grad keys, which release the snap engagement so a single board can be replaced without disturbing the rest of the deck. Mini Rails are a fixed alternative used at board ends.

docs.t: What screws and nails does InvisiClip™ use?
docs.p: InvisiClip™ Hidden Fastener System (Grad System)
docs.d: Type 316 stainless steel screws (#8 or #10, 1.5 inch length, Simpson Strong Tie T08162WPB) for screw fastening, or 0.148 inch by 1.5 inch hot-dip galvanized class D nails (N10D5HDG-R) for nail-gun installation.

docs.t: Has InvisiClip™ been independently tested for wind uplift?
docs.p: InvisiClip™ Hidden Fastener System (Grad System)
docs.d: Yes. American Pro grooved decking installed with InvisiClip™ technology was tested by Intertek Building & Construction (TL-144 IAS-accredited, ISO/IEC 17025) under ICC-ES AC174 Section 4.1.4 using ASTM E330 methods. Three test specimens reached an average ultimate uplift of 306 psf and an average sustained uplift of 292 psf at a 10 second hold before clip release. The full Intertek report R1545.01

docs.t: Which American Pro decking works with InvisiClip™?
docs.p: InvisiClip™ Hidden Fastener System (Grad System)
docs.d: Both decking lines, in the Grooved for InvisiClip™ profile. The same underside channel geometry is extruded on TrueGrain Deck and Legacy PVC Decking, so InvisiClip™ works with either line using the same clips and rails. Standard Grooved Edge boards, which have side slots instead, do not fit InvisiClip™.

docs.t: What is the maximum joist spacing for InvisiClip™?
docs.p: InvisiClip™ Hidden Fastener System (Grad System)
docs.d: Joists must be 16 inches on center maximum, and a rail sits on top of every joist, so rails run at 16 inches on center maximum as well. This follows the Grad System install method.
